For a continuous-time linear time-invariant state model, asymptotic internal stability means every zero-input state response tends to zero as $t\to\infty$. This holds exactly when every eigenvalue of $A$ has strictly negative real part.1
BIBO stability (bounded-input, bounded-output)
A system is BIBO stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output from zero initial conditions. For a proper rational transfer function, this holds exactly when every pole of the reduced transfer function lies in the open left half-plane.2
Stability and Poles

A pole with positive real part gives an exponentially growing response. A pole on the imaginary axis also prevents BIBO stability: a bounded resonant input can produce an unbounded output.

For zero-input state responses, marginal stability allows persistent oscillation. The eigenvalues must have nonpositive real parts, with at least one on the imaginary axis, and each imaginary-axis eigenvalue must have only size-one Jordan blocks. Larger Jordan blocks introduce polynomial growth. This bounded free response does not guarantee BIBO stability.3
A reduced transfer function can also hide an unstable canceled mode, so use the full state model when checking internal stability.1
Necessary and sufficient condition for stability
For a real characteristic polynomial with positive leading coefficient, strictly positive coefficients at every power are necessary for all roots to lie in the open left half-plane. They are insufficient: $p(s)=s^3+s^2+s+2$ has positive coefficients, yet its Routh first column is $1,1,-1,2$. The two sign changes give two right-half-plane roots. Illinois ECE 486, Lecture 7.
In the regular Routh case (no zero first-column entries or all-zero rows), strict stability is equivalent to all first-column entries being positive. Zero entries require the special cases described below before applying the test.

stability 

A zero pivot in a nonzero row can be replaced by a positive $\varepsilon$, with signs evaluated as $\varepsilon\to0^+$. For an all-zero row, form the auxiliary polynomial from the row above and replace the zero row with the coefficients of its derivative. Check the auxiliary roots for imaginary-axis modes; absence of right-half-plane roots alone does not prove strict stability.4
